summary: Rava derives the principle 'ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot' (do not bypass a mitzva) from the Yom Kippur service order - a priest who passes the altar before reaching the menorah must clean the altar first. Abaye's morning service sequence continues: five lamps before tamid blood, blood before two lamps, two lamps before incense, incense before limbs, limbs before meal-offering, meal-offering before libations. Each precedence is derived from biblical language.

glossary.en: Do not bypass a mitzva; when a mitzva opportunity presents itself, one must not pass it by for another opportunity ahead.
Ramp; the inclined ramp leading up to the altar from the south, used by priests to ascend.
Lamps; the seven lamps of the menorah in the Sanctuary.

rashiTranslations.en: But since he enters the Sanctuary, he encounters the altar first - before he reaches the candelabrum, since the altar
is pulled slightly toward the east. Removed from the wall - distanced from the north wall
two and a half cubits, the measure of a path for two priests walking side by side, the ones who arrange the two
arrangements of showbread on Shabbat, whose mitzva is to arrange and clear them together, with four priests
entering, two from this side of the table
to clear away the old arrangement of bread,
and two from the other side to arrange the new one.
Removed from the wall two and a half cubits -
the same measure as the table, since it is written (Exodus 26),
'opposite the table,' each on its own side. Outward -
toward the east, facing the entrance of the Sanctuary. Let us stand it
alongside them - centered directly between them; so why was it pulled
outward? From Reish Lakish - who says one does not
pass over the mitzvot. To forgo the arm phylactery
for the head phylactery - to delay the arm phylactery
for the sake of the head phylactery is forbidden, since
he encounters the arm first. How does he conduct himself,
from the arm to the head phylactery - from the arm he comes
to the head; he places the arm one first and afterward
places the head one. The two instances of 'in the morning'
of the two logs - since they are not needed, as we already said the more atoning act
takes precedence. Cast them here - since this is a principle
in the Torah: a matter with no context of its own is given
the context of another matter. Here three and here
two - here, regarding the tending of the lamps, three instances of
'in the morning' are written, and the one we cast onto it makes
three total; and regarding the daily offering it is written (Exodus 29),
'the one lamb you shall offer in the morning,' and that
one we cast onto it, as stated: one is cast to the blood
of the daily offering. Although here two and here
two - these are the atoning acts, since the burnt-offering atones
for a positive commandment and for a negative commandment convertible
to a positive commandment, as will be explained later in this chapter (36a). If so -
since it precedes the blood of the daily offering, with what do you separate
them, asked to Abba
Shaul, since he holds that the lamps are tended and afterward
the daily offering's blood is offered - the lamp-tending would precede and the incense
would follow later, with what intervening service do you separate them? And if you say,
what does it matter to you - this works out well for Reish
Lakish, who says the pause between them exists only to increase
the sense of the walking of footsteps and the sound marking the start of
the services in the courtyard. Well - you may
say the pause between them is to wait between these
and those, to go out and come in, so that no service
occurs in between. But according to Rabbi Yochanan - who interprets
'in the morning, in the morning' together with 'when he tends,' dividing it into two
lamp-tendings for two mornings, these should precede one service
implying there is a service between them - and this
cannot be said to be filled by the ash-removal of the
inner altar, for if so, since the tending of the five
lamps would precede the ash-removal, he would be passing over
the mitzva; and there is no other service left to bring forward
and place between them, since all of them are ordered
here according to the verses. To the matter that
has only one mention of 'morning' - the daily offering
has 'you shall offer in the morning' stated of it once. And if you say
we cast one of the two-log instances onto it - it is onto the daily offering's blood that we cast it, and not
onto the limbs; and if you say the more atoning act takes precedence, there is no atonement except through the blood. From where do we derive that no matter
may be placed on the large arrangement before the limbs of the daily offering.

The verse teaches - the daf ends mid-comment here; the comment (quoting 'and he shall arrange upon it the burnt-offering' to establish that the burnt-offering must be first placed on the arrangement) continues on 34a.

display.whats: Rava: do not bypass a mitzva (ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot). The priest entering the Sanctuary encounters the altar first and must clean it before reaching the menorah - this teaches the general principle.
display.hint: The order of Temple service is not just practical - it derives the universal principle that when a mitzva is encountered, it must be performed immediately without bypassing it.
display.title: Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot: don't bypass the mitzva in front of you

learning.ahaMoment: Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot is not just a halachic rule about Temple service - it is derived from the physical layout of the Temple and becomes a universal principle: when you encounter a mitzva, perform it immediately. Do not walk past one mitzva to do another.
learning.memoryAnchor: Don't skip past the menorah to reach the altar. First thing encountered = first obligation. This is ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Mishna split the menorah's seven lamps into two separate cleaning sessions - five before the tamid offering, and two after - rather than cleaning all seven together?
learning.coreTension: The menorah's seven lamps and the daily tamid offering compete for sequence: cleaning all seven lamps together before the tamid would be the simplest approach, yet the Mishna's order splits the lamp-cleaning into two groups around the tamid.
learning.coreMove: Reish Lakish explains the split using ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot: the five lamps closer to the entrance are encountered first as the priest enters, so he must tend to them immediately rather than walking past them toward the altar; Rava extracts this as a universal principle that a mitzva encountered first must be performed first, not deferred for a later, more central one.

takeaway.text: Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot is not an abstract maxim - the Gemara grounds it in the literal physical order in which a priest meets each task while walking through the Temple, then generalizes it as the standard for any mitzva encountered in sequence.

learning.learningBlocker: It's tempting to think 'don't bypass a mitzva' is just a vague piety, rather than a precise sequencing rule explaining a concrete halachic division of labor (five lamps, then tamid, then two lamps) in the Temple.

argumentFlow.label: Priest enters Sanctuary - altar or menorah first?
argumentFlow.text: When a priest enters the Sanctuary, he encounters the inner altar (for incense) after passing the menorah. The sequence: menorah is closer to the entrance; altar is further in.

argumentFlow.label: Rava: ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot
argumentFlow.text: Rava concludes from Reish Lakish: do not bypass a mitzva when you encounter it. The priest must clean the five closer menorah lamps before proceeding to the inner altar.

misconceptions.misconception: Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot means you must always do the most important mitzva first.
misconceptions.correction: Actually it means you cannot bypass the first mitzva you encounter to do a different one ahead.

visualizableElements.label: Sanctuary entry and service order
visualizableElements.description: Priest enters from east: menorah on left (south), inner altar further in. Ein ma'avirin: clean menorah first, then proceed to altar.

visualizableElements.label: Skip vs encounter principle
visualizableElements.description: Wrong: walk past menorah to reach altar first. Right: clean menorah lamps encountered first.

quizSeeds.question: What universal halachic principle does Rava derive from the Temple service order?
quizSeeds.answer: Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot - do not bypass a mitzva that you encounter. When a mitzva presents itself, perform it immediately rather than passing it for another mitzva ahead.

quizSeeds.question: How does the Sanctuary's physical layout lead to this principle?
quizSeeds.answer: A priest entering the Sanctuary encounters the menorah before reaching the inner altar. Rather than passing the menorah to reach the altar first, he must clean the menorah lamps he encounters first.

sugyot.finalRuling: Ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot: do not bypass an encountered mitzva for another ahead. This principle governs many areas beyond Temple service.

display.whats: Abaye's service sequence continues: five lamps precede tamid blood; blood precedes two remaining lamps; two lamps precede incense; incense precedes limbs; limbs precede meal-offering. Rav Pappa challenges the five-before-blood order. The Reish Lakish vs R. Yochanan basis for the five-lamp sequence.
display.hint: The sequence follows a pattern: each service creates the proper context for the next. Five lamps set up for the tamid; tamid's blood enables incense; incense enables the limb placement on the fire.
display.title: Defending the lamp-then-blood-then-lamp order against Rav Pappa's challenge

learning.ahaMoment: The morning service sequence emerges from a web of interlocking biblical phrases: 'in the morning, in the morning' (doubled), 'offerings and libations' (paired), and the physical layout of the Sanctuary. All these sources must be honored simultaneously.
learning.memoryAnchor: The sequence flows like a morning prayer: approach (five lamps), central act (blood/tamid), more approach (two lamps), most intimate act (incense before the Presence), then offering (limbs, meal, wine).
learning.learnerQuestion: Could the order of the five lamps, the tamid's blood, and the two remaining lamps just as easily be reversed, given that the same biblical phrase is used to derive both halves of the sequence?
learning.coreTension: Abaye derives both 'five lamps before blood' and 'blood before two lamps' from the same doubled phrase 'in the morning, in the morning,' which raises Rav Pappa's challenge: nothing in the wording itself seems to dictate which 'morning' governs which precedence, so the order could in principle run the other way.
learning.coreMove: Abaye answers on two tracks depending on whose view is followed - Reish Lakish's ein ma'avirin principle locks the order in one way, while R. Yochanan's view that the verse teaches the incense's own timing supports it differently - and the sugya continues building the rest of the sequence (two lamps, incense, limbs, meal-offering, libation) on the same kind of textual anchoring.

takeaway.text: A precedence derived from a textual cue is only as strong as the explanation for why that cue points one direction rather than the other; Rav Pappa's challenge shows that even an established sequence needs its directionality independently justified, not just asserted from the wording.

learning.learningBlocker: A learner can take Abaye's sequence as simply 'the' order without realizing each linkage was actively challenged and had to be defended - the sequence is the product of debate, not an uncontested received list.

argumentFlow.label: Five lamps before blood
argumentFlow.text: Ash removal from five menorah lamps precedes the slaughter and blood service of the tamid - one 'in the morning' applied to the lamps.

argumentFlow.label: Blood before two lamps
argumentFlow.text: The tamid blood service precedes ash removal from the remaining two menorah lamps - the second 'in the morning' applied to the blood.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Pappa: why not reverse?
argumentFlow.text: Rav Pappa: why not apply one 'in the morning' to the blood first (making blood precede all seven lamps)?

argumentFlow.label: Reish Lakish vs R. Yochanan explanations
argumentFlow.text: According to Reish Lakish: ein ma'avirin - the priest encounters the five lamps on the way in and must clean them first. According to R. Yochanan: the morning incense verse requires lamps first.

argumentFlow.label: Two lamps before incense
argumentFlow.text: Ash removal from the two remaining lamps precedes the incense offering - the priest cleans what he encounters before burning the incense.

argumentFlow.label: Incense before limbs
argumentFlow.text: The incense offering on the inner altar precedes the burning of the tamid's limbs on the outer altar.

argumentFlow.label: Limbs before meal-offering
argumentFlow.text: Burning the limbs on the altar fire precedes the sacrifice of the meal-offering accompanying the tamid.

argumentFlow.label: Meal-offering before wine libation
argumentFlow.text: The meal-offering precedes the wine libation - derived from 'offerings and libations' (offering before libation).

misconceptions.misconception: All seven lamps are cleaned before the tamid begins.
misconceptions.correction: Five lamps are cleaned before the tamid, then two more after the inner altar ash removal.

misconceptions.misconception: The incense is burned at the start of the morning service.
misconceptions.correction: It comes in the middle, after the tamid's blood and two lamp cleanings.

visualizableElements.label: Complete Abaye morning sequence
visualizableElements.description: Wood - 5 lamps - Tamid blood - 2 lamps - Incense - Limbs - Meal-offering - Wine libation

visualizableElements.label: Reish Lakish vs R. Yochanan on 5-lamp priority
visualizableElements.description: Reish Lakish: ein ma'avirin (don't bypass encountered lamps). R. Yochanan: incense verse requires lamps first.

quizSeeds.question: In Abaye's morning sequence, what comes immediately before and after the incense (ketoret) offering?
quizSeeds.answer: Before ketoret: ash removal from the two remaining menorah lamps. After ketoret: burning the tamid's limbs on the altar fire.

quizSeeds.question: Why does Abaye say the blood of the tamid comes before the cleaning of the remaining two menorah lamps?
quizSeeds.answer: One of the two 'in the morning' phrases is applied to the blood service, placing it after the five-lamp cleaning but before the two-lamp cleaning.

sugyot.finalRuling: Complete morning sequence: Wood - 5 lamps - Tamid blood - 2 lamps - Ketoret - Limbs - Meal-offering - Wine. Each step's position is biblically or logically derived.
